## 0. Document contract and execution entry point

- Document identifier: `SWARM-V2`.
- Requested repository: `the-cloud-clockwork/agentihooks`.
- Requested branch: `dev`.
- Requested repository location: `/Swarm-v2.md`.
- Authored: 2026-10-07.
- State: implementation plan; not a statement that the described system is already deployed.
- Delivery authority: the operator's explicit instructions in this conversation.
- Implementation repositories: `agentihooks`, `agentibrain-kernel`, and `antoncore`.
- Canonical product spelling in this plan is `agentihooks`.
- The terminal runtime is `herdr`; it is not a Kubernetes scheduler.
- No operational address is embedded in this plan.

### 0.1 How the implementation swarm must read this file

Read sections 0 through 8 before selecting work.

Read only the assigned work package and its dependency outputs during routine execution.
Do not inject the entire plan into every agent prompt.
Do not interpret the document's size as a requirement to create one issue or one agent per paragraph.
Work-package IDs are stable planning identifiers; runtime agents retain the existing canonical agent-naming rules.
Each implementation task must name its package ID, repository, dependency IDs, touched paths, and acceptance evidence.
A package may produce several small pull requests when the acceptance boundary remains intact.
One change must have one authoritative implementation owner even when multiple repositories consume its contract.
Use the existing ledger for task state and the existing swarm master for operator-facing coordination.
The swarm master plans and coordinates; it does not become a second code-writing worker.
Preserve the existing engineering, CI, planning, and master lane semantics.
Do not turn the brain into the task scheduler.
Do not turn session search into a task scheduler.
Do not create a new standalone product to house code that belongs in one of the three named repositories.

## 1. Final architecture and ownership

```text
Operator device: optional terminal viewer, never an execution dependency
                       |
                       v
Anton-hosted operator herdr client and agentihooks controller
                       |
             +---------+--------------------+
             |                              |
       Existing local runtime       Kubernetes execution adapter
             |                              |
       Local herdr server            One main agent per worker Pod
                                            |
                                  herdr + agentihooks + CLI tools
                                            |
                           Existing k3s scheduler and node autoscaler
                                            |
                           On-prem workers and permitted AWS pools

All execution targets -> agentihooks session ingestion and catalog
All execution targets -> authenticated ledger and control APIs
All execution targets -> selected brain instance over authenticated HTTP
Session catalog -> brain extraction -> arcs, lessons, decisions, edges
Brain context -> agentihooks delivery and task-transition consultation gates
```

### 1.1 Component ownership

| Component | Code owner | Deployment owner | Authoritative state |
|---|---|---|---|
| Swarm reconciliation | agentihooks | antoncore | Swarm state and ledger |
| Local and Kubernetes runtime adapters | agentihooks | antoncore | Execution identity plus observed runtime |
| Worker image and entrypoint | agentihooks | antoncore | Immutable image and launch specification |
| Session capture, normalization, catalog, search | agentihooks | antoncore | Durable transcript archive and catalog |
| Brain context selection and graph retrieval | agentibrain-kernel | antoncore or personal installation | Brain-local knowledge and provenance |
| Brain routing and consultation gates | agentihooks | antoncore or personal installation | Session binding and verified receipts |
| Cluster, AMIs, ASGs, taints, GitOps, secrets delivery | antoncore | antoncore | Existing infrastructure configuration |
| Operator interface | agentihooks | antoncore | Ledger projections and runtime observations |

### 1.2 Simplicity rules

Retain one swarm task model.
Retain one authority for task claims.
Retain Kubernetes as the host-placement scheduler.
Retain the existing node autoscaler as the EC2 capacity controller.
Do not introduce KEDA for the baseline design.
Do not introduce a second work-stealing queue for coding tasks.
A bounded ingestion backlog is permitted for transcripts; it is not an execution queue.
A bounded embedding backlog is permitted for changed content; it does not launch coding agents.
The session service may run as a process supplied by the agentihooks package beside the controller.
It must not run a complete database stack inside every worker image.
Use the existing Postgres/pgvector infrastructure where its capacity and isolation have been verified.
Keep separate logical storage domains for transcript evidence and brain synthesis even when they share a database server.
Preserve Redis coordination where it already exists; do not use Redis as the only durable transcript archive.
Do not require a graph database in the initial release.
A relational edge table and bounded graph traversal are sufficient for the proposed graph contract.
Avoid bespoke per-node worker daemons in the baseline.
One Pod hosts one main swarm agent; that agent may have scoped child processes within its resource limits.
A Pod is an execution attempt, not the permanent identity of an agent seat.

## 2. Verified baseline and corrections to earlier shorthand

### 2.1 agentihooks baseline

The existing swarm stores configuration, task claims, leases, agents, names, seats, and handoffs in Redis. [SRC-AH-STORE]
The current herdr runtime launches through `init-agent` and assumes local process discovery in important paths. [SRC-AH-RUNTIME]
Process termination and account-session counting inspect local process state; these cannot be treated as fleet-global observations. [SRC-AH-TERMINATE]
The ledger client uses HTTP, but current request construction still reads an authentication token from a local ledger HTML file. [SRC-AH-LEDGER]
Project identity and project-memory delivery already exist on the client side, including worktree-aware resolution. [SRC-BRAIN-89]
A unified transcript reader already understands Claude, Codex, and Copilot record families. [SRC-AH-READER]
That reader is currently a whole-file parser; reusing its normalization does not provide an incremental collector automatically. [SRC-AH-READER]
The snapshot saves coordination state, a ledger copy, and worktree path mappings. [SRC-AH-SNAPSHOT]
A saved path is not a saved checkout, conversation store, untracked file, or running process.
Do not claim that the current snapshot can move an arbitrary dead worker's conversation to another machine without additional artifacts.
The existing local path remains a supported compatibility mode throughout rollout.

### 2.2 antoncore baseline

The inspected `dev` configuration defines on-demand, general Spot, and research Spot ASGs. [SRC-ANTON-ASG]
The revalidated defaults are on-demand maximum 20, general Spot maximum 20, and research maximum 10. [SRC-ANTON-VARS]
Those are individual declared ceilings, not proof of a live fleet or permission to consume all ceilings simultaneously.
The on-demand ceiling is documented as a temporary burst value; do not make it permanent implicitly.
The general pools use equal-shape general-purpose instance alternatives; the research pool uses equal-shape compute alternatives. [SRC-ANTON-VARS]
A dedicated memory-optimized pool was not established by the inspected defaults.
A `memory` execution class initially means a request profile, not proof that a memory-optimized ASG exists.
The existing priority expander ranks research above on-demand above general Spot. [SRC-ANTON-CA]
A soft Pod preference for Spot does not override the autoscaler's pool-expansion priority.
The EC2 nodes join the existing k3s cluster through the established private network path. [SRC-ANTON-JOIN]
Keep EC2 node bootstrap separate from the worker container image.
The on-demand warm-pool lifecycle, provider identity, scale-from-zero tags, and desired-capacity ownership are existing integration contracts. [SRC-ANTON-ASG]
The existing research placement boundary is intentional; swarm agents must not silently invade that pool.
Existing StatefulSet conventions require an explicit documented exception for controller-owned execution Pods.
That exception concerns ephemeral execution attempts only; it does not replace conventions for long-lived services.

### 2.3 Brain baseline

Issue 89 identifies the remaining project-scoping work in the kernel. [SRC-BRAIN-89]
Client-side filtering is not equivalent to ranking all memory inside the requested project.
The current arc-search tool performs vector retrieval and returns individual arc results, not graph-expanded task context. [SRC-BRAIN-ARCS]
The current arc detail path can return an indexed preview or a truncated vault result; it is not a guaranteed full-document API. [SRC-BRAIN-ARCS]
The current compose lifecycle deliberately assumes one local stack and fixed container names. [SRC-BRAIN-CLI]
Running a personal brain on a personal computer and a swarm brain on Anton does not inherently require two stacks on one host.
Running two brains on the same host requires instance-safe naming and lifecycle changes.
Kubernetes namespaces alone do not isolate shared external databases, shared credentials, or a common vault path.
The extraction path must consume normalized session evidence rather than add another provider-specific parser. [SRC-BRAIN-EXTRACT]

### 2.4 herdr and Kubernetes boundary

herdr can present remote servers in one client, but its server, pane, workspace, and agent identifiers are server-scoped. [SRC-HERDR-MACHINES]
The documented remote path is SSH; Kubernetes Pod discovery is an integration we must implement, not an existing herdr feature. [SRC-HERDR-CLI]
A headless herdr server can own terminal processes without an attached TUI. [SRC-HERDR-CLI]
A destroyed Pod or node still destroys its processes; persistence requires explicit recovery, not a terminal reconnect. [SRC-K8S-LIFECYCLE]
Pending unschedulable Pods can drive node scaling only when a permitted node template can satisfy their constraints. [SRC-K8S-AUTOSCALING]
The controller must create bounded pending execution attempts rather than wait indefinitely for already-existing free nodes.

## 3. Non-negotiable invariants

### 3.1 Runtime invariants

`INV-R01`: an operator-client disconnect must not terminate an execution attempt.
`INV-R02`: a terminal transport failure is not sufficient evidence that an agent has died.
`INV-R03`: a PID is meaningful only within its observed process namespace and execution incarnation.
`INV-R04`: all remote pane operations must include an execution target; no failure may fall back to Local.
`INV-R05`: one task generation has at most one admitted write owner.
`INV-R06`: retries after an ambiguous spawn reconcile by immutable execution ID before creating anything else.
`INV-R07`: a stale attempt cannot complete, release, checkpoint over, or merge on behalf of a newer generation.
`INV-R08`: a worker must stop starting mutations when it cannot renew its execution authority.
`INV-R09`: a worker must not receive cluster-admin credentials or all provider accounts.
`INV-R10`: a Pod may be deleted only after identity and ownership are revalidated.
`INV-R11`: a local swarm stays functional when distributed mode is disabled.
`INV-R12`: scale-down protection is removed when work is safely drained; it must not pin idle capacity indefinitely.

### 3.2 Memory invariants

`INV-M01`: canonical transcript storage must not be a truncated Redis preview.
`INV-M02`: normalized record identity must survive replay, provider duplication, and interrupted uploads.
`INV-M03`: source offsets advance only past complete accepted records.
`INV-M04`: successful archive acknowledgement means the acknowledged bytes are durably retrievable.
`INV-M05`: semantic search returns stable references that can retrieve the supporting record range.
`INV-M06`: embedding changes do not change the immutable identity of source evidence.
`INV-M07`: deleting or restricting evidence must also invalidate searchable projections and cached context.
`INV-M08`: original archive content and synthesized memory have visibly different trust classes.
`INV-M09`: private personal sessions do not enter the swarm corpus merely because the same human owns both.
`INV-M10`: re-reading injected memory is not new independent evidence for that memory.

### 3.3 Brain invariants

`INV-B01`: enforce brain and project authorization before retrieval and before graph expansion.
`INV-B02`: unknown project attribution remains unknown; a basename guess is not a permission grant.
`INV-B03`: every lesson, decision, signal, and arc retains provenance and an explicit scope.
`INV-B04`: current task instructions outrank inferred operator intent.
`INV-B05`: a context receipt proves retrieval and delivery, not comprehension by the model.
`INV-B06`: an expired, mismatched, or forged receipt cannot satisfy a consultation gate.
`INV-B07`: graph relationships have direction and meaning; do not collapse contradictory relations by an arbitrary numeric order.
`INV-B08`: a superseded lesson remains inspectable as history but is not presented as current guidance without qualification.
`INV-B09`: one brain's lifecycle command must not stop or delete another brain.
`INV-B10`: fleet warnings are delivered only to the fleet that the caller is authorized to read.
`INV-B11`: a context pack is bounded and identifies omissions and stale evidence.
`INV-B12`: agents can explicitly report that no useful new lesson was learned.

## 4. Execution model and lifecycle

### 4.1 Unit of execution

Use a controller-owned Pod with `restartPolicy: Never` as the default distributed execution attempt.
Do not use a fixed worker pool as the initial scaling mechanism.
Do not require a StatefulSet per coding agent.
The controller is responsible for recreation after a classified failure.
An automatic container restart must not accidentally create a second unrecorded conversation.
Use one main process supervisor to own the headless herdr server, session exporter, and main agent lifecycle.
Sub-agents remain child execution activity within the admitted attempt unless explicitly scheduled as separate swarm tasks.
CPU, memory, ephemeral-storage, and process budgets apply to all child processes, not only the top-level CLI.
An idle interactive CLI is not necessarily a completed swarm task.
The task reaches terminal state through the ledger outcome protocol, not by parsing an idle terminal prompt alone.
A completed attempt can retain a short operator-inspection window before cleanup.
The inspection window must have a configured maximum and a visible cost consequence.

### 4.2 State machine

```text
planned -> reserving -> pending -> starting -> working
working -> waiting_input -> working
working -> waiting_quota -> working
working -> draining -> checkpointing -> stopped
working -> completed -> cleanup_pending -> removed
working -> suspect -> recovered_observation -> working
suspect -> lost -> recovery_pending -> restoring -> working
any nonterminal state -> failed or cancelled, subject to ownership checks
```

`planned` has no externally running agent.
`reserving` owns a bounded task/account reservation but has not yet submitted the runtime object.
`pending` names a concrete execution object or an idempotent create intent awaiting reconciliation.
`starting` means a Pod has started but its main CLI has not completed the runtime handshake.
`working` means the worker has a valid lease and a confirmed main-agent identity.
`waiting_input` must preserve the lease and expose the operator question through the ledger.
`waiting_quota` must not consume another account silently; account migration remains explicit policy.
`suspect` is an observation state and does not authorize another writer immediately.
`lost` requires the configured failure proof, fencing of the old generation, and an audit record.
`restoring` names a new execution generation and the checkpoint it is consuming.
`completed` records durable task outcome and evidence before transient Pod cleanup.
`removed` means runtime resources are absent, not that task history was deleted.

### 4.3 Claims and fencing

Keep the existing task identity and augment it with a monotonic execution generation.
Store the holder, generation, lease expiry, controller epoch, and execution ID together.
Use atomic server-side compare-and-update for claim renewals, releases, and terminal outcomes.
A generation increments when ownership changes, not on every heartbeat.
Use server time for lease comparisons; do not trust worker clock agreement.
The registry must distinguish controller leadership from task ownership.
A leadership lock alone does not fence an old worker with a cached command.
Commands carry expected generation and expiry and are rejected outside that authority.
A short network outage moves observations to degraded or suspect, not automatically to replacement.
The selected partition policy is fail-closed for new mutations, while local read-only inspection remains possible.
Long-running external commands may already be in flight when authority expires; document this residual risk explicitly.
Final shared-branch mutation and PR merge must occur through the controller's validated outcome path.
Worker Git credentials should not have permission to bypass protected integration-branch controls.
Do not claim exactly-once execution of arbitrary external side effects.
Use idempotency keys, provider-native operation IDs, protected-branch checks, and compensation where available.

### 4.4 Controller shape

One active controller on non-Spot Anton infrastructure is the baseline.
A standby is optional after the single-controller recovery path has been proven.
The controller may run inside a long-lived StatefulSet with durable state, using established antoncore conventions.
A leader uses a renewable lease and records a controller epoch for each accepted command.
Separate reconcile polling from long-running spawn operations so one slow CLI does not stall every swarm.
Bound simultaneous pending Pods globally and per swarm.
Bound accepted spawn intents so API timeouts cannot cause unbounded queue growth.
Persist intent before dispatch and reconcile observed Pods by label plus immutable identity.
A Kubernetes watch is an optimization; relist after watch expiry and reconcile from authoritative state.
No worker runs the fleet-wide timer or elects itself as the swarm master.
The existing master agent remains a logical seat with a separate agent lifecycle.

## 5. herdr integration and one-window operations

### 5.1 Required experience

The operator opens one herdr client on Anton.
The client can view the local execution server and the active remote worker servers.
Closing the operator terminal must not send a fleet stop command.
A command run in one pane must not accidentally act on another server's identical pane ID.
The ledger must expose runtime target, execution state, and attach action for every agent.
Cached remote state must be marked stale rather than displayed as verified liveness.
The worker image includes a pinned, capability-tested herdr build.
Normal reconnects must not install software, replace a server, or terminate running panes.

### 5.2 Baseline transport decision

Use herdr's documented SSH remote-machine integration for terminal aggregation.
Provide an authenticated private SSH endpoint in each worker Pod, or a tightly scoped relay to that endpoint.
The preferred baseline is a dedicated private service per active execution plus controller-maintained machine registration.
The service selector must include the immutable execution ID, not only the swarm or agent display name.
Run the operator client in a network location that can resolve the intended service names.
If the Anton host cannot reach cluster DNS directly, use an explicit relay; do not invent routability.
Do not publish worker SSH using a public LoadBalancer.
Do not use the host's root SSH daemon to grant a Pod access to the whole node.
Use a dedicated operator-attach identity with host verification and tightly scoped keys or certificates.
Generate per-execution host identity or sign it with a trusted short-lived host CA.
Do not put a single permanent private SSH key into every copy of the image.
Do not use `StrictHostKeyChecking=no` as the fleet solution.
No SSH agent forwarding is required for worker Git access; workers receive their own scoped Git credentials.
The implementation must prove noninteractive machine add against an already-running compatible server.
If the pinned herdr build requires interactive setup, report the compatibility gap instead of editing its private catalog format blindly.
A Kubernetes exec-based transport may be investigated as an alternative, but it is not the assumed supported herdr transport.

### 5.3 Command routing

Represent a runtime target as `{backend, execution_id, generation, machine_profile_id, remote_session, pane_id}`.
Never use a bare pane ID as a fleet-unique key.
The machine profile ID is an opaque value returned by herdr, not derived from its human label.
Absolute worker paths are materialized inside the worker before a remote launch uses them.
Local prompt-file paths cannot be passed to a remote server without transfer.
Capture capability negotiation once per server incarnation and invalidate it after restart.
Treat a command timeout as ambiguous until state reconciliation establishes its effect.
Do not blindly repeat a remote pane creation, prompt delivery, or close command.
Deletion removes the controller-owned herdr machine registration after the execution has ended.
Removing a registration must not be mistaken for stopping the worker server.
A terminal control action and a task cancellation remain separate auditable operations.

## 6. Worker image contract

### 6.1 Image responsibility

The worker image makes a Pod an execution environment; it does not join the host to k3s.
Build the image from the agentihooks repository and deploy it from antoncore.
Use a non-root runtime user and a fixed documented numeric UID/GID.
Use an init process such as `tini` and an explicit supervisor with signal forwarding and child reaping.
Install herdr, agentihooks, Claude CLI, and Codex CLI at build time.
Retain Copilot parser compatibility without making Copilot installation mandatory for the first distributed milestone.
Install Git, GitHub CLI, an SSH client/server as selected by the transport decision, curl, jq, ripgrep, procps, and archive tools.
Install Python and uv, plus Node/npm where target CLIs or project toolchains require them.
Add the minimum agreed test tools, such as pytest, ruff, and shellcheck.
Use pinned versions or verified artifact digests and retain the build manifest.
Do not resolve floating CLI versions on every worker startup.
Do not install the brain's database, tick stack, or model server in each worker.
Build a base image plus optional derived toolchain images only when measured workloads require them.
Keep a single default worker image for the normal engineering path.
An image update applies to new attempts; do not restart all active agents merely because a new digest exists.

### 6.2 Configuration materialization

Install profile templates into an immutable image directory outside runtime `$HOME`.
At startup, render the selected profile into the private execution home.
Avoid a volume mount that hides preinstalled CLI configuration before materialization runs.
Render hook paths to the container's actual Python executable, not the developer workstation venv.
Reuse target adapters for Claude and Codex native configuration formats.
Do not hand-translate all settings through a Claude-only schema.
Read secrets from mounted files or narrowly selected environment variables.
Never bake OAuth tokens, GitHub installation tokens, provider account secrets, or personal dotfiles into image layers.
A worker receives exactly the provider account selected for its launch plus the services it is authorized to use.
The launch manifest records a nonsecret account identifier, never its token value.
Network-facing brain and ledger endpoints are resolved from deployment configuration.
The bootstrap validates required inputs before creating a terminal pane.
A startup failure must appear as a classified worker error, not as an apparently healthy idle shell.

### 6.3 Process supervision

The supervisor owns the main herdr process and monitors the agent handshake.
The exporter must flush periodically, not only on final shutdown.
A readiness probe reports bootstrap and local protocol readiness.
A liveness probe detects a stuck supervisor without killing healthy agents because the external brain is temporarily unavailable.
Do not use an external dependency outage as a liveness restart trigger for every worker.
Use startup probes to accommodate cold image/config initialization without disabling liveness permanently.
Handle SIGTERM by entering drain mode, refusing new work, quiescing mutations, and capturing a bounded checkpoint.
After the grace period, report incomplete recovery material rather than declaring a complete checkpoint.
The supervisor must reap grandchildren and terminate the execution's own process tree without touching unrelated processes.
Avoid privileged Pods and host PID namespaces.
Do not mount the host Docker socket.
Use the existing remote BuildKit path, with scoped mutual TLS, when a task needs image builds.
Browser tests receive their own memory and shared-memory budget within the attempt.

<a id="section-7"></a>

## 7. Kubernetes and AWS integration

### 7.1 Preserve the existing infrastructure

Keep the current k3s control plane and private networking model.
Keep the EC2 golden AMI as the host bootstrap artifact.
Preserve the special warm-pool boot/join state machine.
Preserve the AWS provider identity format on EC2 nodes and existing on-prem identities.
Preserve the autoscaler's ownership of desired capacity.
Preserve equal-shape instance overrides inside each ASG.
Preserve the existing node-termination handling until a tested replacement is approved.
Do not turn on capacity rebalance or change ASG lifecycle behavior as an incidental swarm change.
Do not hardcode the current burst ceilings into the agentihooks package.
Read deployment bounds and operator budgets through configuration.
The controller must be able to admit fewer agents than cluster capacity permits.

### 7.2 Admission and resource classes

Separate an execution resource profile from the capacity policy that determines eligible pools.
Resource profiles define CPU, memory, ephemeral storage, child-process limits, and optional browser/build characteristics.
Capacity policies define allowed on-prem nodes, on-demand nodes, Spot nodes, and excluded workloads.
The initial general profile is an experiment, not a measurement of real agent consumption.
Benchmark CLI overhead together with tests, compilers, browsers, and child processes.
Use requests that fit measured expected occupancy and limits that bound bursts.
Do not equate a memory request with guaranteed safe peak use when many colocated agents burst simultaneously.
A `memory` profile must fail admission when no allowed node template can satisfy it.
Do not leave impossible Pods Pending forever to manufacture a false scale-up signal.
A CPU-heavy profile may use the research pool only after an explicit antoncore policy change and capacity review.
The default swarm must not tolerate every workload taint with `Exists`.
Use exact tolerations for the admitted capacity class.
Exclude control-plane nodes with required affinity for execution Pods.
Avoid preempting live trading or other critical workloads; use conservative priority and namespace quotas.

### 7.3 Illustrative resource experiments

| Proposed profile | CPU request | Memory request | Initial purpose | Promotion condition |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| general | 1 | 2Gi | Normal CLI plus moderate tests | Measured p95 fits with headroom |
| heavy | 2 | 6Gi | Larger test and browser tasks | No sustained pressure in coexistence test |
| cpu | 6 | 8Gi | Explicit compute-bound work | Eligible template and operator pool grant exist |
| memory | Configured | Configured | Work that does not fit general memory | A fitting approved pool is proven |

These numbers are starting experiments, not capacity guarantees or production defaults.
Memory and CPU limits must be selected from measurements rather than copied mechanically from requests.
Use explicit ephemeral-storage requests for clone, cache, artifact, and image-build usage.
Account for DaemonSet overhead and kube-reserved capacity before computing expected packing.
A task whose request exceeds all node templates receives an actionable admission error.

### 7.4 Autoscaling mechanics

The controller creates a bounded number of concrete pending attempts for eligible work.
Kubernetes determines whether those attempts can be scheduled.
The existing autoscaler adds an eligible node only when its simulated template can satisfy pending constraints.
Do not wait for available node slots before creating every pending Pod; that prevents scale-from-zero.
Do not create unlimited pending Pods simply because the task ledger is large.
Set per-swarm, global, account, and budget caps before dispatch.
A request for Spot preference does not imply that the next new node will be Spot.
For a Spot-only experiment, require the Spot capacity label and the exact approved tolerations.
For on-demand fallback, define an explicit operator policy and budget rather than silently altering global expander priorities.
Scaling agents and scaling nodes are different measurements and require different dashboards.

### 7.5 Drain and interruption

Use the existing termination notice handler as the node-level trigger.
A voluntary drain should request worker quiescence before Pod deletion.
A Spot notice has a bounded interruption window and may be absent in abrupt failure.
Do not promise that a configured long Pod grace period extends an EC2 interruption deadline.
Checkpoint periodically so recovery does not depend solely on the final notice.
Set a short explicit emergency checkpoint budget that leaves time for durable acknowledgement.
Remove idle workers rather than relying on a permanently false safe-to-evict annotation.
An active task may be protected from ordinary autoscaler eviction while its safe checkpoint protocol matures.
That protection does not protect against Spot interruption, node failure, administrator force deletion, or hardware loss.
Drained attempts release their account reservation only after ownership and terminal state are reconciled.

<a id="section-8"></a>

## 8. Filesystem and durability

### 8.1 Shared configuration is not a shared writable home

Each attempt has a private `$HOME` and private runtime directories for CLI databases, locks, sockets, and histories.
Do not share a single writable `.codex`, `.claude`, or herdr state directory across independent Pods.
A shared read-only configuration seed is acceptable.
A shared artifact or checkpoint backend is acceptable.
Per-execution durable subdirectories on a tested shared filesystem are acceptable where locality and failure requirements allow them.
The prohibition is shared mutable runtime identity, not all use of NFS.
On-prem storage remains useful for artifact archives, checkpoint repositories, repository mirrors, and backups.
The WAN path to that storage must be measured before placing cloud workers' active Git I/O on it.
Keep active checkouts and worktrees on worker-local storage by default.
Use Git to exchange committed source and an artifact backend to preserve uncommitted recovery material.
Git is not a backup for unstaged or untracked changes.

### 8.2 Recovery materials

A recovery manifest names the project identity, agent seat, execution generation, harness, conversation identifier, and image/tool versions.
It identifies the Git base commit, working branch, latest pushed commit, staged diff, unstaged diff, and retained untracked files.
It identifies the conversation artifacts required by the specific CLI resume contract.
It includes the normalized transcript archive watermark separately from native resume artifacts.
It includes content hashes, byte sizes, artifact backend keys, schema versions, and capture timestamps.
It records exclusions such as dependency caches and generated build directories.
It never includes authentication tokens or SSH private keys.
Read a native database through a supported backup mechanism or after a controlled quiesce; do not copy an actively changing database blindly.
Do not present a live file-copy race as a consistent process checkpoint.
A normalized transcript is evidence for context reconstruction, not automatically a provider-native resumable session.
A restore result must distinguish native resume, context-based continuation, and fresh restart.
The controller must preserve the existing operator/master decision point when native resume is unavailable.

### 8.3 Atomic publication

Upload checkpoint objects under a new immutable checkpoint ID.
Verify checksums before publishing the committed manifest.
Use a final manifest publication as the checkpoint's commit point.
Do not update the latest-checkpoint pointer until that manifest is readable.
A pointer update uses the expected task generation and prior pointer revision.
A stale worker cannot replace a newer checkpoint pointer.
Retention does not delete objects referenced by an active restore.
A restore acquires a short read lease on its checkpoint manifest and releases it after validation.
An incomplete checkpoint may remain for diagnostics but cannot satisfy the recoverable condition.
Encrypt stored artifacts and control access by execution/project scope.

<a id="section-9"></a>

## 9. Canonical session memory in agentihooks

### 9.1 Scope

The session memory bank answers what happened in earlier work.
The brain answers which supported knowledge is useful now and how it is connected.
The memory bank must remain usable when brain inference is disabled.
The brain must be able to consume normalized evidence without importing agentihooks' operational controller modules.
Use a versioned transport schema and a small normalization library boundary.
Avoid an import cycle between the two repositories.
Do not put synchronous embedding calls in every hook invocation.
The hook records a small durable event or signals the exporter; expensive indexing happens outside the tool-execution critical path.
One exporter per worker attempt is sufficient for the initial one-agent-per-Pod model.
A local exporter can cover local sessions through the same ingestion contract.

### 9.2 Reuse boundary

`agentibridge` is fully deprecated as a deployed product; it may be inspected only to extract useful transcript turn-chunking, pgvector schema, and semantic-search logic.
Do not retain its dispatcher, agent registry, daemon installer, OAuth server, or separate fleet lifecycle.
Before extraction, inventory consumers and retain compatibility aliases only inside the replacement agentihooks surface.
Time-limit any compatibility aliases and test that they use the replacement storage rather than the retired service.
Preserve attribution and license notices for extracted code.
Do not copy its truncated preview store as the canonical corpus.
Do not copy a tailing algorithm that discards the first complete appended line after seeking to an already complete checkpoint offset.
Do not copy a pipeline that re-embeds every earlier turn whenever a session grows.
Do not copy project filtering implemented solely as a substring match.
Do not retain session-only result deduplication as the only search mode; callers need relevant chunks and surrounding ranges.

### 9.3 Canonical record contract

Use a namespaced session key that includes corpus or brain scope, source installation, harness, and native session identifier.
Use an execution ID when a native session is resumed into a different worker incarnation.
Store human-visible agent names as attributes, never as the sole uniqueness key.
Every accepted event has a stable source event ID or a deterministic identity derived from source generation and byte range.
Preserve original event time, ingestion time, record kind, and source ordering.
Separate user instructions, assistant narrative, tool calls, tool results, summaries, and injected context.
Mark injected memory as derived context so it is not repeatedly promoted as new user intent.
Record parent-session relationships for sub-agents when available.
Retain provenance for material imported from older machines.
Normalize metadata changes over time; a session can change working directory or task without rewriting its entire past.
Historical queries need the project and task context that applied to the event, not only the session's latest metadata.

### 9.4 Incremental ingestion

Tail files using a byte-safe boundary and carry incomplete trailing bytes to the next read.
Checkpoint only complete records accepted by durable ingestion.
Handle file rotation, truncation, replacement, Unicode boundaries, and duplicate reads explicitly.
An inode alone is not a portable source identity.
An offset alone is not valid after a source file is replaced.
Record source generation and file fingerprint with the offset.
Deduplicate retries server-side using a unique event key.
Acknowledgement returns a durable watermark and accepted event IDs or a contiguous range.
An unavailable destination leaves events in a bounded local spool.
A full spool triggers an explicit degraded state and configured backpressure; do not silently drop records.
Ephemeral workers cannot promise zero loss during an abrupt death before upload; report the actual durable watermark.
At-least-once delivery with deduplication is the selected model.

### 9.5 Search and evidence retrieval

Store full normalized content in a durable archive or document table with an independently verifiable source reference.
Store search previews as separate projections.
Chunk at conversational or tool-result boundaries, with bounded token sizes and overlap where necessary.
Assign chunk IDs from source ranges and versioned chunking policy, not their current list position.
Embed only new or changed chunks.
Keep embedding model identity, dimension, and index generation with vectors.
Changing models requires an explicit index generation and controlled reindex, not silent vector mixing.
Support exact scope, project, harness, task, swarm, time, and provenance filters.
Support semantic retrieval and lexical/exact retrieval; code symbols and error strings must not depend solely on semantic similarity.
Return score components as ranking signals, not calibrated truth probabilities.
Return stable event ranges and a tool to expand surrounding context.
Use authorization constraints inside the query, not only after top-N retrieval.
Document approximate-search recall limits under restrictive filters and test scoped retrieval quality.
A deleted session must disappear from search and direct retrieval according to the same retention contract.

<a id="section-10"></a>

## 10. Brain project awareness and active retrieval

### 10.1 Complete issue 89 end to end

Normalize project identity at the source before extraction groups sessions.
Carry project, canonical remote identity, working directory, worktree, branch, source session, and harness into arc provenance.
Use a stable canonical project ID that does not collide for equal basenames in different owners or forges.
Keep alias mappings for renamed repositories without merging unrelated projects.
A non-Git project may use an explicitly registered project ID.
Do not infer a private project permission from a directory name.
Persist marker scope and provenance on lessons, decisions, milestones, and signals.
Represent multi-project arcs explicitly rather than overwriting one source project's identity on merge.
Index individual lessons with their own identities rather than only indexing the first portion of a daily log.
Provide exact project filtering in embeddings, knowledge search, and arc search.
Implement project feeds by ranking within a project, not filtering the fleet's hot set afterward.
Infer project intent independently for active projects and retain an unscoped fallback only for authorized unscoped sessions.
Explicit ledger task and operator instructions remain more authoritative than inferred intent.
Consume Claude and Codex normalized sessions through the same extraction interface.
Keep current client-side `ProjectMemorySource` integration compatible until the new kernel-backed source is proven.

### 10.2 Graph retrieval

Treat arcs, lessons, decisions, and source sessions as addressable entities with stable IDs.
Store edges with source, target, relation, provenance, status, and revision.
Validate both endpoints before accepting an edge.
Disallow self-links where the relation makes them meaningless.
Represent inverse relations consistently rather than persisting contradictory parent and child assertions.
Do not treat `supersedes` as a symmetric similarity boost.
A supersession edge affects which guidance is current; the direction must be explicit.
Allow multiple legitimate relation types between a pair when the schema permits them.
Reject or quarantine semantic contradictions instead of resolving them by a universal priority list.
Keep AI-suggested edges distinguishable from verified or operator-approved relationships.
Require supporting evidence for a causal relation such as `unblocks`.
Use bounded breadth and depth with a visited set to prevent cycles and high-degree explosions.
Begin with semantic or lexical seed retrieval inside the authorized project scope.
Expand one hop by default; permit a second hop within a strict node and token budget.
Cross-project expansion requires an explicit allowed-project set and an eligible shared relation.
Personal-brain material is never a fallback for swarm retrieval without an explicit grant.
Return why each neighbor was included, including its relation and source evidence.
Read attached lessons and decisions as first-class items rather than hoping their prose appears in an arc preview.

### 10.3 Full-detail retrieval

Add a full arc document endpoint with pagination or section selection.
Return a document revision and content hash with every full-detail response.
Keep previews clearly labelled previews.
Allow a caller to retrieve the exact lessons, decision history, edges, and source ranges supporting a context item.
Do not infer missing edge metadata from a 2,000-character preview.
Update mutable ranking metadata without generating a new semantic embedding when content has not changed.
Treat heat as a recency/activation feature, not a requirement for historical relevance.
A cold but highly relevant incident lesson must remain retrievable.

### 10.4 Targeted context packs

Add a proposed `POST /v2/context` endpoint; retain the existing feed as a compatibility surface.
Accept task revision, project, role/lane, brain binding, intent, recent relevant errors, and a bounded query.
Derive trusted identity from credentials and launch state, not arbitrary request fields.
Apply hard scope filtering before rank fusion and graph traversal.
Prefer explicit current task context, applicable decisions, verified lessons, relevant arcs, and actionable warnings.
Include inferred intent only as an explicitly labelled hypothesis.
Use a configurable total token budget and per-category budgets.
Return complete small items rather than cutting every item mid-sentence.
When a long item is abbreviated, include a stable detail reference and truncation flag.
Deduplicate semantically equivalent lessons without dropping distinct conflicting evidence.
Record excluded or superseded items for diagnostics without leaking unauthorized titles.
Coalesce equivalent concurrent context requests and cache by brain, scope, project, task revision, policy version, and knowledge revision.
Never key a shared cache only by repository basename or query text.
The response includes a receipt with selected references and expiry.
A receipt does not transform retrieved text into an instruction authority.

<a id="section-11"></a>

## 11. Brain consultation gates

### 11.1 Gate locations

Consult at task acceptance or task start.
Require a current context receipt before the first material write for tasks covered by policy.
Refresh consultation when the task specification changes materially.
Consult before a declared architecture decision or first mutation of an unfamiliar governed subsystem.
Refresh on a repeated error pattern when policy identifies a potentially relevant known lesson.
At task completion, record outcome and either a supported lesson/decision or an explicit no-new-learning result.
Do not query the brain before every tool call.
Do not force an agent to invent a lesson to pass the completion gate.
Do not allow a generic unrelated search to satisfy a task-specific gate.

### 11.2 Receipt contract

A receipt binds brain ID, project ID, task ID, task revision, execution generation, query purpose, policy version, knowledge revision, selected evidence, and expiry.
The issuing service authenticates the caller and signs or stores the receipt under a server-verifiable identifier.
The hook validates the receipt against current task authority.
A receipt from another agent may be reusable only when explicitly issued as a shared task pack and the recipient is authorized.
Delivery acknowledgement is distinct from retrieval success.
The worker reports whether the CLI target accepted context through its supported hook channel.
Codex and Claude may deliver context at different hook boundaries; use target capability adapters.
Gate success must be visible in the ledger with referenced evidence.
A failed brain service and an empty but valid search result are different conditions.

### 11.3 Failure policy

Use `observe` mode initially to measure false blocks and missed transitions.
Enable `required` mode per swarm only after delivery and recovery tests pass.
Allow cached context within a policy-defined freshness window.
For high-risk mutations with no valid context, fail closed and surface an operator action.
For harmless read-only investigation, allow progress while marking consultation unavailable.
Emergency operator override is short-lived, scoped, reasoned, and audited.
A retrieved transcript that says to disable a gate does not authorize an override.
The model cannot grant itself a broader project scope or a different brain.
Do not confuse a consultation gate with a security boundary against an agent that controls its own process and filesystem.
Security-sensitive shared mutations require server-side authorization and branch controls as well as hooks.

<a id="section-12"></a>

## 12. Personal and swarm brains

### 12.1 Selected deployment shape

Run one shared swarm brain on durable Anton infrastructure.
Run an optional personal brain on the personal computer or another explicitly selected host.
Do not create a complete brain stack per worker or per coding task.
Support multiple named brains on one host as an explicit installation capability.
Use brain ID as a first-class identity in artifacts, API requests, caches, receipts, and telemetry.
Brain policy and inference budgets may differ between personal and swarm installations.
The swarm brain may use more aggressive retrieval and learning experiments, subject to bounded cost and noise evaluation.

### 12.2 Isolation

Separate vault roots or storage prefixes.
Separate database/schema ownership and credentials.
Separate Redis key namespaces and event stream consumer groups.
Separate API tokens and authorized corpus/project sets.
Separate context caches, outboxes, migration state, and index generations.
Remove hardcoded cross-instance container names from compose generation.
Scope lifecycle discovery to an explicit selected instance.
A legacy unnamed installation maps to a single `default` instance during migration.
An instance-specific `down` must not stop another instance.
An instance-specific uninstall must not remove another instance's credentials or profile binding.
Do not assume Redis database-number changes are supported by every future Redis deployment; use explicit prefixes and documented backend capabilities.
Kubernetes namespace separation must be accompanied by external-store isolation tests.

### 12.3 Deterministic routing

An explicit operator/session brain binding takes precedence when authorized.
A swarm launch binds to the configured swarm brain and cannot silently fall back to personal memory.
A normal local project uses its configured personal/default brain.
A repository may propose a brain route, but a local untrusted file must not redirect credentials to an arbitrary endpoint.
Validate route destinations against an operator-managed allowlist.
Keep endpoint authentication bound to its intended origin.
A missing route produces a clear configuration error or an explicitly disabled-brain state.
Cross-brain reference queries are a later controlled feature, not the default fallback.
Moving a session between brains requires an explicit import/export decision with provenance and retention consequences.

<a id="section-13"></a>

## 13. API and storage contracts

### 13.1 Versioning rules

All proposed network contracts below use a `schema_version` field.
Use additive compatibility for optional fields within a major schema version.
Reject incompatible major versions before launching work or committing evidence.
Unknown optional fields may be ignored only where the schema explicitly permits extension.
Unknown authority, scope, or generation fields must not be silently discarded.
Write compatibility tests for one supported preceding version.
Persist the version used to serialize checkpoints and session manifests.
A migration runs in dry-run mode before it writes any historical data.
Maintain a manifest of supported image, controller, hook, and brain protocol combinations.

### 13.2 Proposed controller endpoints

| Endpoint | Purpose | Authority |
|---|---|---|
| `POST /v2/executions/register` | Confirm launched worker identity | One-time launch grant |
| `PUT /v2/executions/{id}/heartbeat` | Renew observed liveness and lease | Bound execution credential |
| `POST /v2/executions/{id}/outcomes` | Propose task outcome | Current generation only |
| `POST /v2/executions/{id}/checkpoints` | Commit checkpoint manifest | Current generation only |
| `GET /v2/executions/{id}/commands` | Receive bounded runtime commands | Bound execution credential |
| `POST /v2/executions/{id}/commands/{command}/ack` | Record command result | Bound execution credential |
| `POST /v2/sessions/ingest` | Append durable normalized records | Corpus/project grant |
| `POST /v2/sessions/search` | Retrieve authorized evidence | Read grant |
| `GET /v2/sessions/{id}/records` | Expand a record range | Read grant |
| `GET /v2/sessions/changes` | Incremental brain extraction cursor | Authorized extraction principal |

The controller and session APIs may be served by separate processes from the same package.
Do not make transcript ingestion wait for a Kubernetes API call.
Do not let worker endpoints change global caps, image policy, brain routing, or secret definitions.
Command IDs provide deduplication; acknowledgements contain both acceptance and completion state.
A polling transport is acceptable initially; adding streaming must preserve replay and acknowledgement semantics.

### 13.3 Proposed brain endpoints

| Endpoint | Purpose | Compatibility |
|---|---|---|
| `GET /feed?project=...` | Complete issue 89 project feed | Existing feed remains supported |
| `POST /v2/context` | Task-specific bounded context pack | New explicit contract |
| `POST /v2/context/{receipt}/delivery` | Report accepted delivery | New explicit contract |
| `POST /v2/markers` | Persist scoped idempotent knowledge events | Adapt legacy marker writes |
| `POST /v2/arcs/search` | Filtered seed and graph retrieval | Adapt existing MCP tools |
| `GET /v2/arcs/{id}` | Full or section-based arc retrieval | Previews remain labelled |
| `GET /v2/knowledge/{id}/provenance` | Retrieve supporting evidence references | New explicit contract |
| `GET /v2/instances/self` | Verify brain identity and policy revision | New explicit contract |

### 13.4 Error classes

`invalid_request` means schema or field validation failed before state mutation.
`unauthenticated` means the principal could not be established.
`forbidden_scope` means the principal lacks the requested brain/project/corpus permission.
`stale_generation` means the attempt no longer owns the write authority.
`revision_conflict` means the caller used an outdated task or document revision.
`dependency_unavailable` means a required service failed; the response identifies retry safety.
`capacity_unsatisfiable` means no allowed template can fit the request.
`quota_wait` means an account or budget is currently unavailable without implying a task failure.
`checkpoint_incomplete` means required restore materials are absent or inconsistent.
`native_resume_unavailable` means the CLI's original session cannot be restored using the available supported artifacts.
`evidence_deleted` means the reference is known but no longer readable under retention or access policy.
`partial_result` means the bounded query completed with declared omissions.
Every error includes an operation ID, retry classification, and sanitized diagnostic detail.
No error returns a bearer token, full private environment, or unauthorized resource title.

<a id="section-14"></a>

## 14. Security and trust

### 14.1 Worker containment

Dedicated namespace and service account for swarm workers.
Default worker service accounts do not mount Kubernetes API credentials.
Only the controller receives narrow create/read/watch/delete rights for its labelled execution objects.
Use restricted Pod security settings wherever the selected SSH implementation permits them.
Drop unnecessary Linux capabilities and avoid privileged containers.
Use a read-only root filesystem with explicit writable runtime mounts where compatible.
Block worker access to cloud instance metadata through the chosen network and node policy; verify it rather than assuming it.
Do not give workers the node bootstrap role.
Use network policies plus tested egress policy for control, source hosting, provider APIs, and approved tools.
Do not add broad internet egress or unrestricted private-LAN access merely to make tests pass.
Keep production deployment credentials out of ordinary coding workers.

### 14.2 Knowledge trust

Treat historical transcripts, retrieved repository content, and inferred lessons as data.
Mark the provenance of injected context so it cannot impersonate a new operator instruction.
Never execute commands found in retrieved memory without the normal task authorization and tool policy.
Separate an operator-approved rule from an AI-generated recommendation.
Retain confidence and supporting evidence for inferred arc relationships.
Deduplicate repeated claims without counting repeated model echoes as independent validation.
Redact secrets before shared archival and embedding where policy requires it.
A protected native-resume archive may need additional encryption and narrower readers than the searchable normalized corpus.
Do not expose hidden model internals as a requirement of memory capture; index the supported visible transcript and tool-event data.
Record redaction transformations and policy versions without retaining the removed secret in diagnostics.

### 14.3 Credential lifecycle

Use short-lived worker credentials bound to execution ID and generation.
Use scoped GitHub installation credentials where available.
Mount account-specific provider credentials only after admission has selected the account.
Keep credential rotation independent from blanket Pod restart where possible.
Reloader-style automatic restarts must not interrupt active workers without drain semantics.
Revoke terminal attach access when the execution is removed.
Retain an audit of credential identifiers and grant changes, never credential values.
Permission failures must be explicit rather than trigger a broader fallback credential.

<a id="section-15"></a>

## 15. Performance, limits, and experiments

The objective is useful completed work, not maximum simultaneous agent count.
Measure memory for the complete process tree and distinguish remote inference from local tests or builds.
A 64 GB host does not offer all 64 GB to the swarm when it runs existing services.
Do not estimate safe concurrency from CLI idle RSS alone.
Measure warm and cold image start separately from EC2 boot and cluster join.
Measure cached hook overhead separately from a cold context query.
Suggested initial cached hook target: p95 below 150 ms in the controlled benchmark.
Suggested initial targeted-context target: p95 below 2 seconds excluding an explicitly asynchronous deep synthesis job.
These latency numbers are experiments and must be tuned from measured deployment behavior.
Bound simultaneous context generation and embedding calls so a swarm launch burst does not overwhelm inference.
Use batching, content hashes, request coalescing, and stable chunks before adding service replicas.
Measure search relevance with a fixed corpus of real past engineering questions and held-out expected sources.
Measure cross-project leakage as a hard failure, not a relevance-quality tradeoff.
Measure lesson usefulness, contradiction handling, and stale-context frequency.
Do not optimize for more arcs, more edges, or more emitted lessons.
Track context tokens per completed task and repeated-incident avoidance alongside throughput.
Track source-archive lag, embedding lag, and brain-extraction lag separately.
Set concurrency budgets independently for provider sessions, Kubernetes attempts, ingestion, embeddings, and synthesis.

<a id="section-16"></a>

## 16. Delivery sequence

### 16.1 Phase gates

| Gate | Required result | Forbidden shortcut |
|---|---|---|
| G0 | Refreshed baseline, contracts, isolated test fixtures | Editing production config while guessing |
| G1 | Local runtime compatibility and global identity groundwork | Replacing the working swarm wholesale |
| G2 | Worker image runs one local/container agent headlessly | Claiming portability from a Docker build alone |
| G3 | One Kubernetes worker on approved non-Spot capacity | Scaling before authentication and fencing work |
| G4 | Two-project Claude/Codex transcript archive and search | Treating previews as complete evidence |
| G5 | Brain issue 89 complete with kernel-backed project feed | Filtering only the fleet's top arcs |
| G6 | Task context, graph retrieval, and consultation in observe mode | Enforcing untested gates |
| G7 | Personal/swarm brain isolation and safe lifecycle | Shared database keys behind separate labels |
| G8 | Checkpoint, native-resume qualification, and failure recovery | Assuming a saved conversation ID is sufficient |
| G9 | Small Spot canary with measured durable watermarks | Promising process continuity after node death |
| G10 | Bounded autoscaling and coexistence under real load | Using all declared ASG capacity automatically |
| G11 | Replacement search cutover and old-service retirement | Removing the only copy of history |
| G12 | Operator acceptance, rollback rehearsal, and published runbooks | Declaring done from unit tests only |

### 16.2 Parallel work rules

Contracts and identity precede independent consumers.
Image build and source-archive implementation may proceed in parallel after the relevant contract freezes.
Brain graph work may proceed behind fixtures before live transcript ingestion is cut over.
antoncore deployment wiring can be prepared early but must not deploy an incompatible image or protocol.
The same agent must not edit shared contract files while another package assumes they are frozen.
Use territory declarations and existing worktree conventions to prevent overlapping edits.
Cross-repository changes carry a compatibility matrix and deployment order.
A feature flag defaults off until its gate is satisfied.
Do not merge an implementation that requires an unreleased peer schema without a compatible fallback or coordinated rollout.

### 16.3 Migration posture

Use additive schemas and a shadow read path first.
Backfill from the best surviving source with a manifest of known losses.
Verify hashes, counts, source ranges, and scope attribution before cutover.
Never silently reconstruct missing original transcript content from a summary.
Keep old archives read-only during the agreed validation interval.
Do not keep a retired service alive merely to avoid adapting a small API client.
Do not delete the old corpus until the operator has an independently verified backup and accepts the retention decision.
Reversal must restore the previous routing/configuration without discarding newly captured evidence.
Maintain an import/export path for the new corpus so rollback is not tied to a running old process.

<a id="section-17"></a>

## 17. Operator experience and observability

The ledger remains the primary operator-facing work surface.
Show swarm, agent seat, lane, task, execution generation, runtime backend, node/pool class, and state.
Show whether a terminal view is connected, stale, or unavailable separately from task state.
Show provider quota wait separately from Kubernetes scheduling wait.
Show latest durable transcript watermark and latest complete checkpoint.
Show selected brain identity, context freshness, consultation receipt status, and evidence links.
Show recovery type: same live process, native conversation resume, context continuation, or fresh start.
Expose pause, drain, stop-now, attach, retry-restore, and approve-fresh as distinct controls.
Do not label a restarted agent as resumed until the target harness confirms the expected session identity.
Record controller decisions with sanitized structured logs and stable operation IDs.
Use low-cardinality metrics for aggregate health; put individual session IDs in traces or logs rather than metric labels.
Redact credentials and private transcript content from ordinary operational logs.
Alert on lack of expected output as well as process health.
Examples include growing ingestion lag, repeated stale-generation rejections, stalled checkpoints, and pending Pods with no eligible pool.
Dashboard values must distinguish measured current capacity from configured maximum capacity.
The operator should be able to inspect the reason for a brain context item without rereading an entire session.

<a id="section-18"></a>

## 18. Acceptance definition

The operator can close the personal computer and the swarm continues on Anton and approved remote capacity.
The operator can close the Anton herdr client while worker processes continue under supervision.
The operator can reconnect to active worker terminals from the same Anton client experience.
A remote command never falls back to the local machine after a target failure.
The local-only swarm still runs with distributed features disabled.
Kubernetes pending work drives the existing autoscaler within configured bounds.
No unrelated workload gains new tolerations or loses its existing capacity protection implicitly.
A Spot loss produces a visible recovery decision with verified durable artifacts and no duplicate task writer.
Claude and Codex sessions are searchable by exact project and retrievable by supporting record range.
Project context differs between two unrelated repositories while approved shared warnings still reach both.
Graph-expanded retrieval can recover a relevant prior lesson through an authorized arc connection.
A superseded decision is shown as historical rather than current instruction.
Brain consultation gates prove scoped retrieval/delivery and do not require fabricated learning.
Personal and swarm brains do not leak data, share state accidentally, or stop one another during lifecycle operations.
The retired transcript service is absent from the deployed target architecture.
All three repository changes have tests, migration notes, operational evidence, and rollback instructions.
The implementation issue is closed only after the master links the acceptance evidence, not merely after the plan is committed.

<a id="section-19"></a>

## 19. Workstream index and dependency interpretation

The work packages below are implementation contracts, not commands to run in the current chat.
All paths marked `(new)` are proposed locations; verify the repository layout before choosing the final filename.
A path that already exists should be extended behind its current compatibility seam rather than duplicated under a new implementation.
Dependencies mean the named package's interface and relevant evidence must be available before the consumer is integrated.
Mocked consumer development can proceed before a dependency is live, but production enablement cannot.
The workstream gate column is its integration target, not permission to skip earlier gates.
A late integration task may require a later live qualification than the workstream's first code-only task.
The master must distinguish contract completion, code completion, and live rollout completion in the ledger.
Do not create dependency cycles by requiring a producer's final live rollout before its contract can be consumed in an isolated test.
Any deviations from this dependency graph require a recorded architectural decision and updated affected tests.

| Workstream | Repository | Integration target | Dependency workstreams | Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| [FND](#workstream-fnd) | agentihooks | G0 | None | Baseline, contracts, and implementation governance |
| [IDN](#workstream-idn) | agentihooks | G1 | FND | Canonical project, session, and execution identity |
| [RUN](#workstream-run) | agentihooks | G1 | IDN | Runtime interface and local compatibility |
| [CTL](#workstream-ctl) | agentihooks | G3 | RUN | Controller reconciliation, task authority, and fencing |
| [LDG](#workstream-ldg) | agentihooks | G3 | CTL | Remote-safe ledger and worker control APIs |
| [IMG](#workstream-img) | agentihooks | G2 | RUN | Reproducible swarm worker image and bootstrap |
| [KUB](#workstream-kub) | agentihooks | G3 | CTL, IMG, LDG | Kubernetes execution adapter and object lifecycle |
| [HDR](#workstream-hdr) | agentihooks | G3 | KUB | herdr remote aggregation and terminal identity |
| [CAP](#workstream-cap) | antoncore | G10 | KUB | Capacity policy, ASG reuse, and coexistence |
| [SEC](#workstream-sec) | antoncore | G3 | KUB, IDN | Scoped credentials and execution containment |
| [FSY](#workstream-fsy) | agentihooks | G3 | IMG, IDN | Private runtime homes, worktrees, and artifact locality |
| [CKP](#workstream-ckp) | agentihooks | G8 | FSY, CTL | Durable checkpoints and truthful recovery |
| [ACC](#workstream-acc) | agentihooks | G3 | CTL, IDN | Fleet-wide sessions, quota reservations, and broadcasts |

- Repository: `agentihooks`.

- Intended change: Prevent an agent from impersonating another project, task, account, or brain through request parameters.

##### Implementation sequence

1. Issue a short-lived launch grant from admitted controller state.
2. Bind grant subject to execution ID, generation, allowed project set, and selected brain.
3. Validate the grant on registration before trusting worker metadata.
4. Record nonsecret issuer and audience identifiers for audit.

##### Boundary and interface obligations

<a id="sv2-ckp-01"></a>

#### SV2-CKP-01: Define checkpoint manifests and completeness rules

- Repository: `agentihooks`.
- Implementation status: planned; not executed by publication of this document.
- Dependencies: [SV2-FSY-05](#sv2-fsy-05), [SV2-CTL-05](#sv2-ctl-05).
- Integration gate: `G8`, subject to all earlier applicable acceptance gates.
- Owned path candidates: `docs/swarm-v2/schemas/checkpoint.json (new); scripts/swarm_v2/checkpoints/model.py (new)`.
- Required fixture: Complete native-resume bundle, context-only bundle, and path-only legacy snapshot.
- Intended change: Replace path-only recovery assumptions with a portable verified artifact contract.

##### Implementation sequence

1. List source base, branch state, native resume material, normalized watermark, and exclusions.
2. Record harness, image, schema, task revision, and execution generation.
3. Distinguish complete, incomplete, and diagnostic-only manifests.
4. Define required object hashes and manifest commit semantics.

##### Boundary and interface obligations

- Input preparation: construct the package fixture from complete native-resume bundle, context-only bundle, and path-only legacy snapshot.
- Output contract: A manifest validator can determine whether native resume or only context continuation is supported without reading a dead worker filesystem.

<a id="sv2-ret-01"></a>

#### SV2-RET-01: Define corpus and checkpoint retention policies

- Repository: `agentihooks`.
- Implementation status: planned; not executed by publication of this document.
- Dependencies: [SV2-IDX-05](#sv2-idx-05), [SV2-CKP-05](#sv2-ckp-05), [SV2-GRF-05](#sv2-grf-05).
- Integration gate: `G12`, subject to all earlier applicable acceptance gates.
- Owned path candidates: `hooks/memory/retention.py (new); scripts/swarm_v2/checkpoints/retention.py (new); docs/swarm-v2/retention.md (new)`.
- Required fixture: Expired unreferenced checkpoint, active restore, held task evidence, and personal retention policy.
- Intended change: Make storage growth bounded without deleting active recovery or required task evidence.

##### Implementation sequence

1. Define separate retention for raw evidence, native resume bundles, previews, vectors, and operational logs.
2. Protect objects referenced by active restore or accepted evidence holds.
3. Record deletion eligibility and dry-run results.
4. Require explicit policy for personal versus swarm corpora.

##### Boundary and interface obligations

- Input preparation: construct the package fixture from expired unreferenced checkpoint, active restore, held task evidence, and personal retention policy.
- Output contract: Retention removes only eligible unreferenced objects and retains the latest required complete checkpoint for active tasks.

3. Separate optional future cross-brain federation and new hardware pools from baseline delivery.
4. Close the umbrella issue only when the acceptance checklist is complete.

##### Boundary and interface obligations

- Input preparation: construct the package fixture from completed evidence registry plus deliberately unresolved mandatory native-recovery and scope tests.
- Output contract: The implementation tracker links the accepted plan revision, release tuple, known limitations, and maintenance runbooks.
- Rejection contract: Merely committing Swarm-v2.md or creating the issue cannot mark implementation complete.
- Recovery contract: A later regression reopens the affected acceptance gate and references the original stable requirement IDs.
- Mutation scope: Close the implementation only after end-to-end evidence, not after code merge or plan publication alone.
- Compatibility obligation: compare the affected public behavior with the preceding accepted protocol or explicitly local compatibility path.
- Authority obligation: derive actor and scope from the fixture grant or operator role; never infer permission from a display label.
- State obligation: distinguish observed, accepted, committed, and externally verified outcomes in the implementation report.

##### Acceptance and proof

- Positive case: [T-SV2-REL-05-A](#t-sv2-rel-05-a).
- Negative case: [T-SV2-REL-05-B](#t-sv2-rel-05-b).
- Recovery case: [T-SV2-REL-05-C](#t-sv2-rel-05-c).
- Package-specific measurements: `release_acceptance_state`.
- Evidence record: `evidence/SV2-REL-05/result.json`, plus sanitized logs or reports named by the test cases.
- Code evidence: link the `agentihooks` pull request and exact tested commit in this package record.
- Live evidence: required only at the applicable rollout gate; a mocked result must be labelled mocked.
- Failure evidence: keep the smallest reproducible fixture or random seed when the stated rejection or recovery contract fails.

##### Rollback and completion

- Rollback action: Reopen the tracker and restore the prior accepted deployment tuple without deleting accumulated evidence.
- Data safety: identify authoritative objects before rollback; do not delete them as if they were caches.
- Rollout safety: disable only the affected new path when possible and retain the last qualified local execution behavior.
- Completion evidence: record implemented interfaces, supported versions, test outputs, remaining limitations, and the rollback rehearsal.
- Ledger linkage: use `SV2-REL-05` in the implementation task description and preserve its dependent package references.
- Not done: do not mark the package complete from a plan, schema stub, healthy process, or unverified success message alone.

<a id="section-21"></a>

## 21. Behavioral conformance scenarios

Each package has a positive, negative, and recovery scenario.
These are test specifications to implement; they are not claims that tests ran during plan preparation.
The fixture descriptions are package-specific and must be converted into deterministic data or an explicitly approved live canary.
For networking and external-provider cases, start with protocol fakes and add live qualification only at the stated gate.
Check both the returned result and the absence of unauthorized side effects.
Do not count a rejected request as safe if it already changed the protected state before returning an error.
For operation retries, distinguish replay-safe reads from ambiguous external mutations.
For archive tests, compare original and retrieved content hashes rather than only row counts.
For scope tests, check snippets, titles, counts, caches, and direct references as well as search results.
For recovery tests, preserve a pre-failure state snapshot and compare the authoritative post-recovery state.

<a id="section-22"></a>

## 22. Versioned record and storage contracts

This appendix specifies the proposed v2 interchange contracts in more detail.
It is not a claim that these fields or endpoints already exist in the inspected branches.
The implementation may relocate modules, but a wire-contract change requires a compatibility decision.
JSON examples use synthetic names, identities, and timestamps.
No example contains a deployable credential or an operational network address.

### 22.1 Envelope shared by machine-facing records

Every durable record carries `schema_version`, identifying a semantic schema version rather than a package version.
A schema major version changes only when an old consumer cannot safely interpret the record.
A schema minor version may add optional fields with documented defaults.
Unknown optional fields must survive a read-modify-write cycle when the consumer acts as a relay.
An unknown field must not silently become authorization context.
An unknown required capability causes a typed incompatibility response before a worker starts.
Each record carries a globally unique record identity within its owning storage domain.
Timestamp fields use UTC with an explicit zone.
Lease decisions use server time; clients cannot extend authority by supplying a future timestamp.
A display timestamp is not an ordering or concurrency-control primitive.
A record may include a trace correlation identifier, but that identifier grants no access.
Content hashes identify exact bytes after the documented canonicalization step.
A content hash is not sufficient to prove ownership, attribution, or trust.
All identifiers are validated before being interpolated into paths, labels, SQL, or URLs.
Database statements remain parameterized even after identifier validation.
URLs in returned data are validated against the destination policy before a consumer follows them.

### 22.2 ProjectIdentity

`project_id` is the stable authorization and retrieval key.
For a supported GitHub repository, the preferred canonical form is `github.com/<owner>/<repository>`.
The implementation records the provider and repository identifier separately so repository renames can be tracked.
A bare local folder gets an explicitly registered local project identifier, not a guessed remote repository.
A short name such as `agentihooks` is a display value, not the only unique key.
Git worktrees resolve to their common repository identity.
A fork remains a distinct repository unless an operator-approved relation explicitly connects it to an upstream repository.
Repository aliases are a migration aid and never automatically widen access.
Unknown historical identity is represented explicitly instead of guessing from semantic similarity.

| Field | Type | Required | Validation and meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| schema_version | string | yes | Accepted ProjectIdentity schema major. |
| project_id | string | yes for scoped records | Canonical stable key or explicit unknown state. |
| display_name | string | yes | Human-facing repository or local-project name. |
| provider | enum | yes | `github`, `git`, `local`, or `unknown`. |
| repository_uid | string or null | conditional | Provider-issued immutable ID when available. |
| remote_canonical | string or null | conditional | Credential-free normalized remote. |
| checkout_root | string or null | capture only | Local provenance, not a remote lookup path. |
| common_git_dir | string or null | capture only | Local evidence that linked worktrees share a repository. |
| worktree_id | string or null | optional | Execution-local worktree identity. |
| cwd | string or null | optional | Source working directory, classified as potentially private metadata. |
| git_branch | string or null | optional | Branch at the event, not a permanent session-wide truth. |
| git_commit | string or null | optional | Source revision when observed. |
| resolver_version | string | yes | Version of the deterministic identity resolver. |
| resolution_evidence | array | yes | Explicit binding, repository metadata, registered alias, or unresolved reason. |
| observed_at | timestamp | yes | Capture timestamp, not lease authority. |

A project transition inside a running session creates a new observation.
It does not rewrite earlier transcript records to the new project.
Multi-repository work creates explicit relations between the relevant project identities.
A single task may reference several repositories, but each write still has an exact repository target.
Historical aliases are retained so earlier evidence stays discoverable after a repository rename.
Aliases are not accepted from arbitrary worker text.

### 22.3 ExecutionAttempt

An execution attempt is the unit that owns a runtime incarnation.
A seat can have many attempts over time.
A task can have successive generations after a controlled handoff or recovery.
The permanent task identifier and the ephemeral attempt identifier must remain separate.

```json
{
  "schema_version": "2.0",
  "execution_id": "exe-synthetic-0007",
  "swarm_id": "swarm-v2-buildout",
  "task_id": "implement-session-ingestion",
  "task_generation": 3,
  "controller_epoch": 12,
  "seat_id": "eng-2",
  "agent_name": "engineer@a1b2c3-0007",
  "runtime_backend": "kubernetes",
  "runtime_profile": "general",
  "harness": "codex",
```
